title: Under the broom tree (1 Kings 19:1–8)
hookLine: exhausted, Elijah wants to die; an angel says eat and sleep
carry: the journey is too great for you

cards: One chapter after fire falls from heaven, Elijah is running for his life.

Ahab tells Queen Jezebel everything that happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a message: by this time tomorrow, you'll be as dead as the prophets you killed. And the man who stood alone against a crowd simply runs.
The text says "he arose, and went for his life." To Beer-sheba, in Judah. He leaves his servant there, walks one more day, alone, into the wilderness, and sits down under a desert bush.

teach.h: IT IS ENOUGH; TAKE AWAY MY LIFE.
teach.b: Under the bush, Elijah asks to die. In the King James Bible: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers."
The King James calls the bush a juniper tree; other translations say broom tree. The Bible doesn't hide this moment. A prophet who has just seen fire from heaven is so spent he wants it all to stop.
Some readers find that honesty a comfort in itself. He lies down and sleeps.
An angel touches him and says only: "Arise and eat." By his head there's "a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water." He eats, he drinks, and he lies down again.
The angel lets him. Then a second touch, and the line we carry today: "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." No argument.
No lecture about Carmel. No correction of his prayer.

teach.h: A CAKE, WATER, AND SLEEP AGAIN.
teach.b: First sleep, then bread and water, then sleep again, then more bread. When the angel finally speaks about the road ahead, it's to agree with him: yes, this is too much for you.

teach.h: THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.
teach.b: Not as a rebuke. As a reason to eat. He "went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God."
The big conversation waits until he has been fed.

One more thing, said plainly: if tiredness ever turns into wanting your life to end, that's the moment to tell someone today, a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line: in the US, call or text 988; anywhere else, your local emergency number.

how: Some Christians turn to Elijah under the broom tree in times of burnout or depression, and pastors sometimes point to the angel's care, food and sleep before any words, as a model for caring for the exhausted.

games.q: you're the angel. a worn-out prophet lies under a bush in the desert. he has just said: it is enough, take away my life. what do you do first?

games.why: bread, water, sleep, and a second touch: "arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee."

practice: Ask yourself three plain questions, the angel's kind: When did I last eat something real? When did I last drink water? How did I sleep?
Don't judge the answers, and set one pressing decision gently to one side until after a meal and a night's sleep; if you pray, rest in the words arise and eat.

wordCard.voice: broom tree. The desert bush where spent and afraid, Elijah asked to die, and an angel answered with bread, water, sleep, and a second touch.

orig.note: Hebrew: the desert bush Elijah sat under (1 Kings 19:4); the King James says juniper, other translations say broom.

carryVoice: Your line: the journey is too great for you. The angel brought bread before any advice. Rest well.
